title: Planning a new website? Start with the decisions that matter
excerpt: Define your website’s purpose, scope and content before commissioning a redesign, with practical questions to bring to your first agency conversation.
author: Paertner
seoTitle: A better website starts with a clearer brief
seoDescription: Define your website’s purpose, scope and content before commissioning a redesign, with practical questions to bring to your first agency conversation.
body:
## Your website should make the next decision easier

You know the website needs work, but deciding what to change is less straightforward. Perhaps your business has moved on while the pages still describe an older offer. Perhaps visitors ask questions the website should already answer. Before commissioning a new design, identify the business problem you want the project to address. That gives you and your agency something more useful to discuss than whether a page feels modern.

Imagine a growing consultancy that offers three distinct services but presents them as one broad promise. The issue may be clarity rather than a lack of pages. A better starting question is: can a prospective client recognize their situation, find the appropriate service, and understand how to begin? This is an illustrative scenario, not a claim about a client result.

## Choose a primary audience and action

List the people who use the website and the reason each person arrives. A prospective customer, a returning client, and a potential recruit do not need the same journey. Choose the audience that matters most to the current project, then describe what that person needs to understand before taking action.

Keep the primary action concrete: ask about a service, request a conversation, or explore relevant work. Supporting actions can still exist. The aim is to give the page a clear hierarchy so that visitors are not asked to make five equally prominent decisions at once.

## Separate essential scope from attractive extras

Build a first-release list around the journeys you actually need. Service pages, useful project examples, contact information and a manageable editing system may matter more than a complicated interactive feature. If a feature depends on content or an integration you do not yet have, record that dependency before treating it as a launch requirement.

Ask what each proposed feature contributes. Who will use it? What must it connect to? Who maintains it? A clear answer helps you compare proposals on their substance. It also makes it easier to discuss which work belongs in the first release and which could follow later.

## Treat content and editing as part of the build

Gather your service descriptions, approved imagery, examples of work and common customer questions before layout decisions become fixed. Where content is missing, agree who will create it and when. A beautiful page still needs something specific to say.

Think about the people who will edit the finished website. They may need to replace images, publish articles, update a service or change a team member’s details. Our [website and web app service](/services/websites-web-apps) brings those everyday responsibilities into the same conversation as design and development.

## Bring this to your first conversation

- Your main business priority for the website
- The audience you most want to help
- The questions visitors need answered
- Essential pages, features and integrations
- Content you already have and content still needed
- Who will approve the work and maintain the site

You do not need a perfect specification to start. A short, honest outline is enough to expose the important questions. If customer discovery is part of the challenge, read our guide to [planning content around customer questions](/blog/seo-starts-with-customer-questions).

## Work toward a brief you can act on

A useful brief is a shared basis for decisions, not a document that pretends every answer is known. It should help the team understand what matters, identify unresolved questions, and keep choices connected to the purpose of the website. As the work develops, revisit the brief when scope or priorities change.

If you have a website that no longer reflects your business, [tell us what needs to change](/book?service=Websites%20%26%20web%20apps#contact-form). Share the current URL, your main concern and what a useful next step would look like. We can start with those details and work through the questions together.

title: What should your business write about for SEO?
excerpt: Find useful article and service-page topics in real customer questions, then build a focused content plan your team can maintain.
author: Paertner
seoTitle: SEO starts with the questions your customers ask
seoDescription: Find useful article and service-page topics in real customer questions, then build a focused content plan your team can maintain.
body:
## Start with the conversations you already have

When a business decides to work on SEO, the first question is often what to publish. A long list of topic ideas can look productive without making the next decision any easier. Start closer to the customer: what do people ask before they understand your offer, compare their options, or feel ready to contact you?

These questions give an article a practical job. A reader should leave with a clearer understanding of their situation, whether or not they make an inquiry immediately. That is a stronger editorial brief than simply asking someone to write about a broad industry term.

## Group questions by the decision behind them

Collect questions from sales discussions, inquiry forms and the people who deliver your service. Keep the wording customers use where it helps reveal a point of confusion. Then group related questions by the decision they support.

For example, someone asking what a website project includes may be exploring the process. Someone asking who prepares the content may be checking responsibilities before choosing a partner. One broad service page can introduce the offer, while an article can explore that responsibility in more depth. This example describes a possible content structure, not a promised search result.

## Give every page one clear purpose

For each proposed page, write a single sentence explaining who it helps and what it answers. If two page briefs are effectively the same, consider combining them before creating separate drafts. Different phrasing does not always mean a different reader need.

Decide how the page fits into the rest of the website. An article can link to a service when that service is a useful continuation of the topic. A service page can link back to an explanation for readers who need more context. Our [SEO service](/services/seo) considers content planning alongside the website structure that supports it.

## Give writers the information only your business can provide

A useful content brief includes more than a title and a target length. Explain the audience, the question, the boundaries of your offer and any details that must be checked. Include real process information and examples your team is allowed to share.

Be careful with claims. If a result has not been measured or a project is only a concept, say so. Specific, honest information is more useful to a reader than an impressive statement that your team cannot support. Ask the person responsible for the service to review the article before publication.

## Build a plan that someone can maintain

- Choose a small set of customer questions to address first
- Assign a purpose and owner to each page
- Record the internal pages it should connect to
- Identify facts, examples and permissions that need checking
- Write a clear search title and description
- Set a review point when the service or process changes

A manageable plan leaves room to improve existing pages. Publishing something new is not the only useful action. Sometimes the better next step is clarifying an important service page or updating an explanation that no longer matches how the business works.

## Choose a useful next question

SEO content should sit within a wider understanding of your audience and website. A question-led plan does not guarantee a ranking, but it gives every piece of writing a reason to exist and makes editorial decisions easier to discuss. If the website itself is unclear, our [website planning guide](/blog/a-better-website-starts-with-a-clearer-brief) can help you frame that part of the work.

If you are unsure what your business should write about first, [share your website and the questions customers ask](/book?service=SEO#contact-form). We can use that context to discuss the content and search work that would be most useful to explore.

title: Social media that fits your business, not just your calendar
excerpt: Plan social content around useful themes, realistic production time and a clear approval process instead of filling a calendar for its own sake.
author: Paertner
seoTitle: Build a social content rhythm your team can sustain
seoDescription: Plan social content around useful themes, realistic production time and a clear approval process instead of filling a calendar for its own sake.
body:
## Recognize the planning problem before increasing output

You want the business to show up consistently, but the social calendar becomes another urgent task each week. Ideas arrive late, images are difficult to find, and a short post can spend days waiting for approval. Adding more publishing dates will not resolve those responsibilities by itself.

Start by looking at how content gets made. The aim is a repeatable process that gives useful ideas a place to go. A realistic plan should survive a busy delivery week, a team member being away, or a period when there is no new announcement to share.

## Choose themes that answer a business need

Select a few themes connected to what customers need to understand. A service company might explain a part of its process, answer a recurring question, and show the thinking behind an approved piece of work. Each theme should help readers recognize what the business does or how it approaches a problem.

Avoid choosing a theme only because it is easy to fill. If a post could come from almost any business, ask what information or perspective would make it yours. You do not need to turn every post into a pitch, but you should know why it belongs in your communication.

## Build a small library of repeatable formats

A repeatable format gives the team a starting point. That might be a question and answer, a short sequence explaining a process, or one photograph accompanied by a useful observation. The format can stay familiar while the subject changes.

Consider the materials available to you. A team with a library of approved photographs can plan differently from a business that needs to commission every image. Be explicit about permissions and where assets come from. Our [social media service](/services/social-media) connects editorial planning with the practical work needed to produce and manage the content.

## Make approval predictable

Decide who prepares a post, who reviews the details, and who can approve publication. Keep the number of reviewers proportionate to the subject. A routine process explanation may need a different review from a sensitive company announcement.

Keep approved source material in one place: service information, imagery, terminology and answers to common questions. A shared library helps writers start from information the business already trusts. For consistency across writers, use the practical approach in our [brand voice guide](/blog/a-recognizable-brand-voice-needs-practical-rules).

## Use a realistic planning checklist

- Name the audience and purpose of each editorial theme
- Choose formats your team can produce with care
- Gather approved imagery and source information
- Assign production, review and publishing responsibilities
- Leave room for timely questions and conversations
- Agree when to review the plan and what to learn from it

Discuss capacity before committing to a schedule. If the work repeatedly arrives late, look at the process and available time rather than treating the calendar as the only measure of success. A smaller plan that your team understands is a more useful starting point than a full calendar nobody can maintain.

## Start with a rhythm you can support

A social plan should make the business easier to recognize and the work easier to organize. Review whether posts reflect the offer accurately, what questions they generate, and which parts of production need attention. Use that discussion to decide what to keep, change or stop.

If social content feels fragmented or difficult to sustain, [tell us about your channels and current process](/book?service=Social%20media#contact-form). Bring examples of the work you like, the material you already have, and where production tends to get stuck. Those details give us a practical place to begin.

title: Before you launch an ad, check where the click goes
excerpt: Review the promise, landing page and contact experience together before committing more effort to your next campaign.
author: Paertner
seoTitle: Connect every campaign to a useful landing page
seoDescription: Review the promise, landing page and contact experience together before committing more effort to your next campaign.
body:
## Follow the same journey your prospective customer will take

An advertisement can attract attention while the page behind it leaves visitors with unanswered questions. Before launching a campaign, follow the complete journey yourself: read the message, open the destination, understand the offer, and take the next step. Look for places where the conversation changes unexpectedly.

For example, a campaign about one service may send people to a homepage describing everything the business does. The visitor then has to find the relevant information again. A more focused destination can keep the offer clear without requiring a complicated page.

## Check that the promise survives the click

Write down what someone could reasonably expect from the advertisement. Does the destination explain that same offer? Does the first section make clear who it is for and why the visitor is there? Consistency matters more than repeating every phrase exactly.

Look for missing qualifications too. If an offer has a particular scope, audience or condition, give that information an understandable place in the journey. A landing page should help people decide whether the offer suits them, not leave the important details until after an inquiry.

## Answer the questions raised by the offer

Build the page around what a prospective customer needs to know next. Explain the scope, the process and the information they need to provide. Show relevant evidence where you have it, and label illustrative examples clearly. Do not use a concept as if it were proof of a measured commercial result.

The right amount of content depends on the decision. A simple introduction may need less explanation than a complex service. Our [paid media service](/services/paid-media) considers the creative and the destination together so that the page is part of campaign planning from the start.

## Make the contact step feel considered

Choose the information your team needs to respond usefully. Every form field should have a reason to be there. If the visitor is only asking for an introductory conversation, avoid making them complete a detailed project specification before they can reach you.

Explain what happens after submission and provide a clear confirmation. Test validation messages, required fields and the return path if something goes wrong. A finished visual design is only one part of the experience; the interaction needs the same attention.

## Run a practical pre-launch review

- Match the advertisement to the destination heading and offer
- Check that the page answers the main customer questions
- Confirm that claims and examples are supported
- Complete the form on a phone as well as a desktop
- Check error messages and the submission confirmation
- Confirm who receives the inquiry and who responds

Use test information for this review and keep it separate from real inquiries. Involve the person responsible for answering the leads so that the handoff is understood. If the destination needs rebuilding, our [website service](/services/websites-web-apps) explains the wider design and development work.

## Improve the journey as a whole

When a campaign needs attention, consider the relationship between message, audience, page and response process. A useful review looks at where uncertainty enters the journey instead of assuming that one new design or one new advertisement will solve every problem.

Planning a campaign or reviewing an existing one? [Send us the offer and the page you plan to use](/book?service=Paid%20media#contact-form). We can discuss how the pieces fit together and where a clearer customer journey could start. For the wider planning context, read about [bringing marketing and your website into one plan](/blog/bring-your-website-and-marketing-into-one-plan).

title: Does your brand sound like the business clients actually meet?
excerpt: Build practical writing guidance that helps your website, campaigns and everyday communication sound consistent without becoming repetitive.
author: Paertner
seoTitle: A recognizable brand voice needs practical rules
seoDescription: Build practical writing guidance that helps your website, campaigns and everyday communication sound consistent without becoming repetitive.
body:
## Look for the gap between the website and the conversation

Your team may explain the business clearly in a meeting, while the website sounds broad, formal or difficult to recognize. Different writers may describe the same service in different ways. A brand voice project can start by identifying those gaps rather than searching for a new slogan.

Gather examples from the places customers encounter your words: service pages, proposals, inquiry replies and social posts. Ask which examples sound like the business people actually work with. Those observations provide useful raw material for a guide your team can apply.

## Translate broad qualities into writing choices

Words such as confident and approachable mean different things to different people. Turn each quality into a practical choice. Confidence might mean describing the scope precisely and avoiding claims you cannot support. Approachability might mean explaining an unfamiliar term rather than assuming the reader already knows it.

Use the reader’s situation as a check. What do they need to understand at this point, and how much context do they have? The same business can sound welcoming in a service introduction and direct in a form instruction without losing its identity.

## Use real examples from your own communication

Choose a few common writing tasks and show how your guidance applies. A service introduction, a project summary and an inquiry confirmation can reveal more than a long list of abstract adjectives. Explain why the examples work so that a writer can make a similar decision in a new situation.

For instance, a vague statement about complete solutions could be replaced with a clear explanation of the work included and who it helps. The point is not to make every sentence shorter. It is to give the reader the information they need without making them interpret an unclear promise.

## Keep the offer and evidence consistent

Voice is connected to substance. If the website describes one process and the proposal describes another, a style guide alone cannot resolve the difference. Agree on the service information, responsibilities and claims that writers can rely on.

Our [brand and content service](/services/brand-content) brings writing decisions together with the places they will be used. If several people create your social content, the [social planning guide](/blog/build-a-sustainable-social-content-rhythm) can help you connect voice guidance to production and approval.

## Create a guide people will actually open

- Describe the reader and the situations you write for
- Turn three or four voice qualities into practical choices
- Include approved examples for common writing tasks
- Record important service terms and phrases to explain
- Clarify which claims need evidence or approval
- Give one person responsibility for keeping the guide useful

Keep the guide easy to find and review it with the people who will use it. Ask them to try it on a real piece of writing. Where they still hesitate, add an example or clarify the rule. A useful guide supports judgment rather than trying to dictate every sentence.

## Make the next piece of writing easier

A recognizable voice develops through consistent decisions across real communication. You do not need to rewrite everything at once. Start with a few important pages or messages, agree on what works, and use them as a reference for the next piece of content.

If your website does not sound like your team, [share a few examples with us](/book?service=Brand%20%26%20content#contact-form). Tell us where the language feels wrong and what clients understand after speaking with you. That contrast can be a useful starting point for clearer brand communication.

title: Your website and marketing should work toward the same next step
excerpt: Connect your website, search content, social activity and campaigns around a customer journey your whole team can understand.
author: Paertner
seoTitle: Bring your website and marketing into one plan
seoDescription: Connect your website, search content, social activity and campaigns around a customer journey your whole team can understand.
body:
## Start with the disconnect your customer experiences

A business can have a well-designed website, active social channels and several campaigns while still feeling fragmented to a prospective client. The customer moves between those places; your team may manage each one separately. A connected plan starts by looking at that experience from the outside.

Consider a business introducing a new service. Its social posts discuss the launch, but the service page is difficult to find and the inquiry form does not mention the offer. Each piece may have an owner, yet the overall journey still needs attention. This is an illustrative planning example, not a report of a client engagement.

## Choose one shared priority

Agree on the business priority before assigning a long list of channel tasks. You might need to explain a new offer, reach a more specific audience, or help existing prospects understand the work. Write the priority in language that the people creating the website and marketing can both use.

Then decide what a useful next step looks like for the customer. It could be reading a relevant explanation, exploring a service, or sending a focused inquiry. A shared objective makes it easier to judge whether a proposed activity belongs in the plan now or can wait.

## Give each part of the journey a useful role

Map how someone might discover you, learn enough to assess the offer, and decide whether to contact you. An article can explore a question. A social post can introduce an idea. A service page can explain the offer and its scope. These roles can complement each other without repeating the same content everywhere.

Check the links between those parts. Is there an obvious continuation when someone wants more detail? Does the destination match the message that brought them there? Our [digital marketing service](/services/digital-marketing) starts with that wider relationship between the work and the decision it supports.

## Plan responsibilities, not only deliverables

A connected plan needs to explain who owns the source information, prepares the content, approves it and handles the response. Otherwise, an apparently simple campaign can depend on a page that has not been written or a form nobody has tested.

Identify dependencies early. If a campaign needs a new landing page, put that work into the plan before scheduling the launch. If an article needs technical input from your team, agree when that review can happen. The [campaign landing-page guide](/blog/connect-campaigns-to-useful-landing-pages) offers a practical review of this handoff.

## Build a focused first phase

- Name the audience and the business priority
- Define the customer’s next useful step
- Map the pages and channels supporting that step
- Identify missing content and technical dependencies
- Assign owners for production, approval and inquiry response
- Agree what to review once the work is in use

You do not need to launch every channel at once. Choose a first phase that your team can deliver and maintain. Write down what is deliberately outside the phase so that a growing list of ideas does not quietly become an unrealistic commitment.

## Use the plan to make the next decision

The value of a shared plan is that people can use it. When a new idea appears, ask whether it helps the audience take the agreed next step. When something is not working as expected, review the whole journey instead of treating every channel as a separate problem.

If your website and marketing feel disconnected, [tell us what you are trying to move forward](/book?service=Digital%20marketing#contact-form). Bring the current website, the channels you use and the main concern. We can use those details to discuss a practical starting point that connects marketing and making.
